RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

Receive and file the February 2025 monthly investment activity reports for the City of
Palmdale and Successor Agency.

BACKGROUND

Pursuant to Section 16 of the City and Successor Agency Investment Policy, the City
Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on investments to
the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The reports shall
detail the type of investment, issuer’s name, purchase date, maturity date, amount of
deposit, and interest rate. This information shall be provided for all City and Successor
Agency pooled investments and for Certificates of Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax
Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts, and Community Facilities District accounts
managed by outside Fiscal Agents.

The monthly investment reports provide a synopsis of the City and Successor Agency’s
investment activity. They provide information on assets, allocations, average maturities,
yields, and book valuations. The interest rates presented are the most current rates
available as of the date of this report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable sources of market prices.

DISCUSSION

Compliance with Investment Policy

For February, the City’s invested portfolio totaled $320,901,760, a decrease of
$4,782,522 from the previous month and an increase of $3,010,544 compared to the
prior year. The monthly decrease resulted from the transfer from Local Agency
Investment Fund (LAIF) to the general bank to cover operating expenditures of the
current month.

The par value of Successor Agency’s portfolio as of February was $10,172,677. The
balance decreased by $2,012,652 from the prior month due to debt service payments
paid during the month.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs, Corporate
Notes, US Treasury Securities, and Government Agency Paper, each adhering to
portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entities’ investment policies: 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient liquidity
to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash requirements; and,
3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on is providing liquidity to meet the
City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the City invests in two
pooled funds, Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) and the California Asset
Management Program (CAMP). These are intended for daily operational activities and
can be used during economic uncertainties for ongoing operating and maintenance
needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the City and Successor
Agency meet cash flow requirements.

The City’s LAIF balance at the end of February was $110,008,322, a decrease of
$5,000,000 from the prior month due to the transfer of funds from LAIF to the City’s
general bank account to fund ongoing operating expenditures of the current month.

The Successor Agency’s LAIF balance at the end of February was $3,857,312, with no
changes from the prior month.

The City’s CAMP balance at the end of February was $52,169,146 compared to
$51,989,186 in January. The increase is due to gained interest during the month.

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report. As of February 28, 2025, the interest rates for LAIF and CAMP investments were
at 4.333 percent and 4.51 percent, respectively. By comparison, the LAIF and CAMP
interest rates at the end of January were 4.366 percent and 4.55 percent. This time last
year, LAIF and CAMP rates were at 4.122 percent and 5.50, respectively.

Diversity

The Finance Division aims to diversify the investment portfolios to avoid incurring
unreasonable and avoidable risks regarding specific security types or individual financial
institutions.

The City and Successor Agency’s investment portfolios remain strongly diversified. The
monthly reports include all investments held by both entities and current book values as
of February 28, 2025.

The City and Successor Agency are expected to have sufficient funds to meet its
expenditure requirements for the next six months. The Finance Division will continue to
monitor current economic conditions and the impact on interest rates.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Second Amendment to Agreement No. A-7526 with Taft Electric
  Company for electrical services, increasing the agreement by $394,137 for a total
  not to exceed amount of $664,137 for a three-year and eleven-month term through
  July 31, 2025; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or designee to execute Second Amendment to
  Agreement No. A-7526 with Taft Electric Company, including minimal and/or non-
  substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

The pathway lights at DryTown Water Park are original to the park, and current fixtures
cannot be updated to accommodate LEDs. Under the terms of the existing contract with
Taft Electric Company for as-needed electrical services and repairs, a quote was
obtained to procure and replace 100 units in the amount of $394,137.

DISCUSSION

Replacement light fixtures are required to properly convert DryTown Water Park
pathway lighting. The new LED fixtures are more energy-efficient, provide enhanced
illumination for better visibility, and contribute to improved safety. Additionally, these
fixtures align with other parks throughout the City, creating a more cohesive and uniform
appearance. Ensuring the lighting is replaced before the start of the 2025 season will

  I.  Intent of City Council

  A.  The present municipal code authority as set forth in Section 2.08.010 of
Title 2 of the Palmdale Municipal Code establishes an automatic, district-based,
numerical rotation for both the office of Mayor and for Mayor Pro Tem. This structure
removes the proper discretion of the entire City Council as regards the selection of
Mayor and Mayor Pro Tem.

  B.  The City Council desires to annually exercise its discretion, and even from
time to time in the course of the term defined by the calendar year, commencing in
January of each year and terminating at the end of December of that calendar year.

  C.  All legal prerequisites to the adoption of this ordinance have occurred as
required by law, and per Palmdale Municipal Code Sections 1.06.040 through and
including 1.06.070, of Title I.
  II.  Ordinance

  SECTION 1. In all respects as set forth in Part I above of this Ordinance which

  SECTION 2. The presently adopted Section 2.08.010 of Title 2 of the Palmdale

  SECTION 3. A new Section 2.08.010 of Title 2 of the Palmdale Municipal Code,
to read in words and figures as follows; is hereby adopted and will be effective thirty
